transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Well, thank you, it's nice to meet you. I came in because... I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It's like I have to jump up and do the next thing, even when I am completely worn out and I know I should just be sitting still. 

I try to sit down, you know, maybe watch a little television. My neighbor, Susan, she lent me these DVDs of that British baking show. She's always bringing things over. Just Tuesday she brought over a green bean casserole, which was sweet of her, but it had so much salt in it. I told her, "Susan, I can't eat all that salt," but she never really listens. She’s got her own hands full, honestly, her grandson just moved back into her basement and he leaves his muddy shoes right on her good rug. It’s a shame, really, because it's a beautiful rug she got at an estate sale. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the sitting still. I just can't seem to do it, no matter how tired I am.

Can you tell me more about this feeling of not being able to sit still—does it ever happen even when you’re not stressed or excited, and do you feel a constant sense of restlessness or pressure inside?

Well, yes, it's all the time. Even on a perfectly quiet day when I have absolutely nothing to be stressed about. It's just this... this pressure inside. Most days I move right from the garden—and oh, my tomatoes are doing terribly this year. I think the aphids got to them before I could even put the soapy water down. I told the boy at the hardware store, I said, "You sold me bad soil," but he just gave me a blank look. Young kids working there these days, they don't know a single thing about gardening. 

But anyway, I go from the garden, straight to the senior center, then I'm off doing church errands, and then I'm back home sorting through stacks of papers on the dining table without even taking a real breath. It just feels like if I stop moving, everything will just completely fall apart. Which reminds me, doing those church errands, Pastor Dave asked me to pick up the little plastic communion cups, and you wouldn't believe how expensive they've gotten! They used to be just a few dollars for a box, but now with inflation and everything being shipped from overseas... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, the pressure. Yes, it's just a constant motor running, even when I'm not excited about anything.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, even for days at a time?

Down? Hopeless? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I still enjoy all my usual things! Like my cross-stitching, I still love doing that, well, when I can actually get myself to stay in the chair for two seconds. Right now I'm making a lovely little bib for my niece’s new baby. She’s having a girl, finally, after three boys! Can you even imagine the grocery bills in that house? Those boys eat like absolute horses. 

Last time I visited, they went through a whole family-sized box of Cheerios before noon. And the milk! They must buy it by the crate, which is just so heavy to carry in from the car. I remember when the milkman used to just leave it right on the porch in those nice glass bottles. The birds used to peck at the foil caps if you didn't get out there fast enough to bring them inside. We had these blue jays in our old neighborhood that were just completely fearless, they would swoop right down at your head if you got too close to the oak tree. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, feeling sad. No, I don't feel sad or hopeless at all. I have plenty of things I like doing, I just... I just can't seem to stop moving long enough to do them properly.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem, like finances, health, or responsibilities, and does this worry happen more often than not?

Worrying? No, not really. I don't sit around fretting about things. Like finances, you mentioned—my Social Security comes right on time every month. Direct deposit is just a wonderful invention, isn't it? 

I remember when you had to take the paper check all the way down to the bank. The line on the first of the month was always out the door! I used to go to the First National on Main Street, before they closed it down and turned it into that trendy coffee shop. They charge seven dollars for a cup of coffee now! Can you imagine? Seven dollars! And they don't even use normal mugs, it's all those little cardboard cups that burn your fingers. I bought one of those reusable cups once, the nice insulated ones with the little slider on the lid, but I left it right in the shopping cart at the grocery store. I called them about it, and the manager, Greg—he's a nice boy, went to high school with my nephew—he went out to check the parking lot but it was already gone. People will just take anything these days, even a used cup! 

But... oh, what was the question? Worrying? Right. No, I don't really worry about much of anything. I'm not an anxious person, I just have that motor running all the time, you know?
Do you ever notice physical symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or shaking along with that inner restlessness you described?

Racing heart? Sweating? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. Well, I mean, I sweat when I'm out in the garden, naturally, especially with how hot it's been lately. Last week was just an absolute scorcher! The weatherman on Channel 4—oh, what's his name, the one with the terrible toupee? It looks like a small animal just resting right there on his forehead. I don't know why the station manager doesn't say something to him. If my husband, God rest his soul, had ever tried to leave the house looking like that, I would have marched him right back to the bathroom. 

We were married forty-two years, you know. We went up to the Poconos for our honeymoon and it rained the entire time. Just absolute buckets of water! We ended up playing gin rummy in the cabin for three days straight. I actually still have that deck of cards in my kitchen junk drawer, the one with the little mallard ducks on the back. The drawer is completely jammed shut right now though, I think a spatula got wedged in the back and I just haven't had the patience to jiggle it loose. I keep meaning to ask my nephew to look at it when he comes over, but he's always in such a rush... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, shaking and sweating. No, no, my heart is fine and I don't shake or anything like that. It's just that constant need to be moving that I told you about.
Do you find that this constant need to keep moving or stay busy is making it hard for you to complete tasks, relax, or function the way you need to in your daily life?

Well, yes, actually. It's... it's gotten to be quite a problem. I just can't seem to sit down and finish anything I start! Like my paperwork and the bills, I used to be so good at keeping the checkbook balanced. But now, my family has had to step in and take over all of that because I just leave piles of mail everywhere. I'll open a bill, set it on the counter to go find a pen, and then I see the counter needs wiping, and then I'm in the laundry room... and the bill just sits there! 

My daughter bought me one of those nice organizers, the ones with the little colored tabs for each month? It's sitting in the hall closet right now, completely empty. I put it in there because the cat kept chewing on the plastic edges. He’s a Maine Coon, you know, just massive, and he chews on absolutely everything. We had to hide all the phone charger cords because he’d bite right through them. I don't know why animals do that, you'd think they'd get a shock or something! My neighbor's dog used to eat rocks, which just seems terrible for your digestion. They had to take him to the vet and pay heaven knows how much for surgery. 

But, oh, what was I saying? Right, the bills. Yes, my family handles them now. And it's not just that. It's happening at church, too, and with my garden club. I'll volunteer to organize the spring plant sale or handle the bake sale committee, and then I just... drop the ball. I get so restless I can't sit through the planning meetings, or I start five different projects for it and finish none of them. The other ladies have had to step in and redo my plans or just cover my responsibilities at the last minute. 

It's just awful. I feel so embarrassed about it. I've been with the garden club for fifteen years! We planted those beautiful hydrangeas by the library, the blue ones—well, they're blue if you put the right acid in the soil, otherwise they turn pink, which is pretty too, but the blue is just striking. But anyway, it just breaks my heart because these are groups I really care about, and now I feel like they can't even count on me anymore.
Do you find it hard to focus on one thing at a time or get easily distracted while trying to complete tasks?

Oh, absolutely. It's nearly impossible for me to just focus on one thing. Like, if I'm sitting down trying to sort the bills or my paperwork at the kitchen table... well, first of all, that kitchen table is right by the big bay window. We put that window in back in '98 because the kitchen was just so dark in the mornings. My husband found the most beautiful custom drapes for it, but they're getting a bit faded now from the sun. I should really look into replacing them, maybe with a nice floral pattern? I saw some lovely fabric at the craft store the other day when I went in to buy thread for my granddaughter's Halloween costume. She wants to be a bumblebee this year! Can you imagine? A teenager wanting to be a bumblebee instead of something scary. 

But anyway, I'll be there at the table trying to focus on the paperwork, and then I'll hear a car door slam outside, and I just have to look and see who it is. Usually it's just the mail carrier, or the neighbors across the street—the Millers. They just bought a new Buick, very flashy red. I don't know why anyone would want a red car, it just screams "pull me over," doesn't it? My first car was a sensible beige. 

Or my cell phone will light up on the table, and I'll glance at it. Half the time it's just one of those scam calls about Medicare. They are so persistent! I tell them, "Take me off your list," but they never do. And if it's not the phone or a noise outside, I'll just get a thought in my head about the garden—like wondering if I remembered to water the petunias—and boom, I'm completely off track. I'll get up to check the flowers, find a weed that needs pulling, and completely forget the bills were even on the table until I go back into the kitchen to make supper! It's just exhausting.
Looking back, did you start feeling this way before you were 12 years old—like you had trouble sitting still, staying focused, or felt driven to keep moving?

Before I was twelve? Oh my, that is going back a ways, isn't it? Let me think... well, yes, actually. Even back in grade school, I remember my teachers always writing notes on my report cards. And those report cards were the thick paper ones, you know? Not like the digital things they have now. My grandson, he just logs into a "portal" on his iPad to see his grades. An iPad! When I was his age, we had those heavy wooden desks with the inkwells still carved into them, even though we only used pencils. 

My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins—she was a lovely woman, wore these cat-eye glasses on a little pearl chain—she was so strict about penmanship. We learned the Palmer method, with all those big, sweeping loops. Nobody teaches cursive anymore, which is just a crying shame if you ask me. How are these kids going to sign a check when they grow up? Though I suppose nobody writes checks anymore either, do they? I still use them at the grocery store, and the young cashiers always look at me like I've handed them a dinosaur bone. They have to call the manager over just to figure out how to run it through the register! It takes twice as long, but I just prefer having the carbon copy for my records. 

But... oh, goodness, what was I talking about? Mrs. Higgins! Right, right, the report cards. Yes, she and all my other teachers used to write that I was a bright girl but just so careless. I was always losing my papers and assignments, or talking out of turn when we were supposed to be reading quietly. They were constantly having to remind me to please stay in my seat and finish my work. So I suppose I've always been this way, just a busybody who couldn't stay put!

But... oh, goodness, what was I talking about? Mrs. Higgins! Right, right, the report cards. Yes, she and all my other teachers used to write that I was a bright girl but just so careless. I was always losing my papers and assignments, or talking out of turn when we were supposed to be reading quietly. They were constantly having to remind me to please stay in my seat and finish my work. So I suppose I've always been this way, just a busybody who couldn't stay put!
